rumi.title: Rumi quotes on love, longing and letting go
rumi.description: Rumi quotes from the Masnavi and the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, in plain English: on love, on something bigger than you, on hard times, on liking yourself, on worry, on letting go and on the long view. Each one names the book it comes from.
rumi.ogDesc: Lines from the Masnavi and the Divan, grouped by what you might need them for. Each one names the book it comes from.
rumi.heroAlt: A sand dune at dusk under a dark sky full of stars
rumi.lede: Rumi wrote about love, longing and a self far bigger than it looks, in Persian, in the thirteenth century. These are his lines in plain English, grouped by what you might need them for, and every one names the book it comes from.
rumi.keywords: rumi quotes, rumi love quotes, rumi quotes on love, rumi quotes about life, masnavi quotes, rumi poems
about: Jalal al-Din Rumi was a Persian poet and Sufi teacher. He was born in 1207, traditionally in Balkh, in what is now Afghanistan, and spent most of his life in Konya, in what is now Turkey, where he died in 1273.

His two great works are the Masnavi, a long poem of stories and teaching in six books, and the Divan of Shams of Tabriz, a collection of lyric poems named for the wandering mystic who became his closest friend.
rumi.source: Each line is rendered into plain, current English from public-domain translations: E. H. Whinfield's abridged Masnavi (1898), and R. A. Nicholson's Selected Poems from the Divani Shamsi Tabriz (1898) and his Mathnawi (1926 and 1930). Many lines shared online as Rumi's are loose modern versions, or not his at all. These stay close to what the old translators found on the page.

sections.love-your-people: Most of Rumi is love poetry, and not only the romantic kind. These are for the people you would cross a desert for.
sections.something-bigger-than-this: His other great theme: that you are part of something much larger, and that it is closer than it looks.
sections.youve-done-harder-things: For the stretch that hurts. Rumi keeps coming back to the same picture: the spring already hidden inside the winter.
sections.like-yourself-today: Lines to read on a day you have been hard on yourself.
sections.when-the-worry-wont-sit-down: For the thought that will not let go. Several of these are about where you put your attention, and what you let float past.
sections.let-a-little-go: On putting things down, and how much lighter the walk is afterward.
sections.the-long-view: On growth that takes its time, and a road that is longer than one bad day.

marcus-aurelius.title: Marcus Aurelius quotes from the Meditations, in plain English
marcus-aurelius.description: Marcus Aurelius quotes from the Meditations, in plain English: on letting go, on trusting your own judgment, on treating people well, on worry, on work, on the present moment and on a good life.
marcus-aurelius.ogTitle: Marcus Aurelius quotes, in plain English
marcus-aurelius.ogDesc: Lines from the Meditations, grouped by what you might need them for.
marcus-aurelius.heroAlt: A dark headland rising over waves breaking on a black sand beach
marcus-aurelius.lede: Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire, and at night he wrote notes to himself about staying calm, fair and kind while he did it. These are lines from those notes, the Meditations, in plain words, grouped by what you might need them for.
marcus-aurelius.keywords: marcus aurelius quotes, meditations quotes, stoic quotes, marcus aurelius meditations
about: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 until his death in 180 AD. He spent much of his reign on military campaigns, and in those years he kept a private notebook, written in Greek and probably never meant for anyone else.
We know it as the Meditations. It is a Stoic's reminders to himself: what is in his control and what is not, how to treat difficult people, and how short life is.
marcus-aurelius.source: Each line is rendered into plain, current English from George Long's public-domain translation of the Meditations (1862).
marcus-aurelius.sourceTranslated: Each line was first rendered into plain, current English from George Long's public-domain translation of the Meditations (1862), and then translated from that English.

sections.let-a-little-go: Marcus spends a lot of the Meditations talking himself out of anger. Most of it works just as well on a bad day at work.
sections.trust-your-own-judgment: On keeping your own counsel when everyone around you has an opinion.
sections.be-easier-to-be-around: Notes on how to treat people, from someone with more power over people than almost anyone alive.
sections.when-the-worry-wont-sit-down: The Stoic move, again and again: what troubles you is your view of the thing, and a view can change.
sections.feel-better-about-work: Including his note for the mornings you do not want to get up.
sections.come-back-to-right-now: He comes back to the present moment more than to any other idea.
sections.meaning-quietly: A good life, as Marcus saw it, is mostly small: be good today, and be glad when something small goes well.
